findings.issue: NCII_SLA is 24 hours; the rule gives 2 hours from the complaint. services/grievance/intake.py line 19 uses this constant as the due time for the intimate_imagery and impersonation categories, so every such ticket is due 22 hours after the deadline in the rule. PAGE_AFTER on line 8 is 12 hours, so the follow-up page also fires after the 2 hours have passed. 24 hours is the period that applied before 20 February 2026. The queue is paged on intake and config/oncall.yaml shows the safety-priority rota as 24x7, so staffing is in place; the clock is the gap.
findings.recommendation: Set NCII_SLA to 2 hours and PAGE_AFTER to a point well inside it (30 minutes, say), recompute due times for open tickets, and check that the reviewer step in ncii.action() can be finished inside 2 hours at night. Consider disabling access on intake, pending review, for these two categories.

findings.issue: The runbook's target is removal within 36 hours of the order reaching the inbox, and it says orders that arrive outside rota hours are picked up on the next working day; the rule gives 3 hours from receipt of the order or intimation. Line 24 escalates only when the 36-hour target is at risk. The runbook was last reviewed in August 2025, before the 3-hour clock took effect on 20 February 2026. The removal action (takedown.remove_on_order) and the audit log exist, so the gap is the stated target and the process around it. Unconfirmed part of this rule: G.S.R. 775(E), which rewrote the rest of rule 3(1)(d), was not read when the catalog was built, so who may issue an intimation and what it must contain are unconfirmed. The 3-hour clock is confirmed.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the Target and Escalation sections around 3 hours from receipt at any hour: who checks the order, who runs remove_on_order(), and when the General Counsel is called (at 90 minutes, say). Drop the next-working-day rule, and put a time limit on step 2, where counsel asks the sender to clarify before acting.

findings.issue: The legal-orders rota covers Monday to Friday, 10:00 to 18:00 IST, and pages by email to the legal inbox; the rule gives 3 hours from receipt, at any time. An order that arrives at 18:01 on a Friday is not seen for about 64 hours. The safety-priority, safety and lea-liaison rotas in the same file are 24x7, so this is the only route to an hours-long clock that sleeps. Unconfirmed part of this rule: G.S.R. 775(E) was not read when the catalog was built, so who may issue an intimation and what it must contain are unconfirmed. The 3-hour clock is confirmed.
findings.recommendation: Give legal-orders 24x7 coverage paged by pager, or route orders to the 24x7 lea-liaison or safety-priority rota with authority to run takedown.remove_on_order() and counsel on call behind them.

findings.issue: Orders sent by post go to the address on the Contact page, which is the Singapore office (web/templates/contact.html line 24 tells senders to use it). The runbook says that office scans post once a week and forwards it to the legal inbox, so a posted order can wait up to 7 days before anyone on the rota sees it; rule 3(1)(d) gives 3 hours from receipt. The runbook also names counsel on the legal-orders rota as the person who receives and confirms orders (lines 7 and 16). Rule 3(2)(a)(ii) puts receiving and acknowledging orders, notices and directions on the Grievance Officer, and no Grievance Officer is named in the reviewed material (see F-0005). Rated above the default for rule 3(2)(a)(ii) because the weekly scan shows the clock cannot be met for a posted order. Unconfirmed part of rule 3(1)(d): G.S.R. 775(E) was not read when the catalog was built, so who may issue an intimation and what it must contain are unconfirmed.
findings.recommendation: Publish an address in India and a monitored email or portal for orders, have post opened daily in India, and name the Grievance Officer as the recipient who acknowledges each order on receipt. Record the time of receipt in the orders register so the 3-hour clock has a start.

findings.issue: The grievance page gives a role mailbox and the report form but 0 names; the rule needs the name of the Grievance Officer and that officer's contact details published. The page speaks only of 'our grievance team', and the acknowledgement and closure emails are signed 'Neem Square Grievance Team'. web/templates/contact.html names a Chief Compliance Officer and a nodal contact person, each stated as based in India, but no Grievance Officer. As a significant social media intermediary the company also needs a Resident Grievance Officer, an employee resident in India, doing this job; none is named and no page says where that person resides.
findings.recommendation: Name the Resident Grievance Officer on the grievance page, with contact details and a statement that the officer is an employee resident in India. The role mailbox can stay as the contact as long as the name sits beside it.

findings.issue: The grievance page is 3 clicks from home: Home, then Help in the footer, then Legal and safety (web/templates/help.html line 9), then Grievance redressal (web/templates/legal_index.html line 5). The rule needs the details on the home page or on a page reached directly from it, which is 1 click at most. The footer on the home page links Terms, Privacy, Community Guidelines, Help, Contact, Transparency and Merch, but not the grievance page, and the Contact page only sends complaints back to Help. The report form is 2 clicks from home.
findings.recommendation: Add a 'Grievance Officer' link to the footer nav pointing at /help/legal/grievance, and put the officer's name and contact details on the Contact page as well.

findings.issue: resolve_days is 15; the rule gives 7 days from receipt. services/grievance/intake.py line 22 turns this value into the due time for the copyright, account and other categories. The escalation job pages 12 hours before that due time, so it first fires on day 14, a week after the deadline in the rule. 15 days is the period that applied before 20 February 2026.
findings.recommendation: Set resolve_days to 7 or lower. Open tickets keep the due_at stored at intake, so recompute due_at for them when the value changes.

findings.issue: content_removal_hours is 72; the rule gives 36 hours from the report for a complaint that asks for removal under rule 3(1)(b), other than sub-clauses (i), (iv) and (xi). services/grievance/intake.py line 21 applies this value to the content_removal and synthetic_media categories. 72 hours is the period that applied before 20 February 2026. A removal request filed under 'Something else' lands in the other category and gets the general clock on line 5, not this one.
findings.recommendation: Set content_removal_hours to 36 or lower, recompute due_at for open tickets, and have triage move a removal request filed under other into content_removal on the day it arrives.

findings.cross_reference: DPDP Act s.8(7) and s.12 erasure: this job may exist to honour erasure. nodal reports the IT Rules gap and does not say which duty wins: see Vigil.
findings.issue: KEEP_REMOVED is 30 days; the rule gives 180 days. The job runs nightly (config/schedules.yaml line 5) and, for every post with status removed, deletes the stored media, the moderation_events rows, the comments and the post row. services/moderation/takedown.py shows that removals on an order, on a grievance, for a guidelines breach and for copyright all set that status, so each is purged 150 days early together with its associated records. Only the audit_log row survives. A side effect: jobs/compliance_report.py counts proactive removals from moderation_events on the 1st of the month, after the purge has deleted the rows for removals made on the first day or so of a 31-day month, so that published count comes out low.
findings.recommendation: Keep removed posts, their media and their moderation records for at least 180 days from removal, longer where a court or agency asks: raise KEEP_REMOVED to 180 days, or move the material to a restricted evidence store and purge from there. Hiding it from users is enough; deleting it is not. Have counsel settle the DPDP overlap before changing the job.

findings.cross_reference: DPDP Act s.8(7) and s.12 erasure: the job says it exists to keep the Privacy Policy's deletion promise. nodal reports the IT Rules gap and does not say which duty wins: see Vigil.
findings.issue: GRACE is 30 days; the rule gives 180 days after the registration is cancelled or withdrawn. Line 14 deletes the signup_records row (the email, phone, date of birth, signup IP and signup time fields) and line 15 deletes the users row 30 days after closure, nightly per config/schedules.yaml line 9. web/legal/privacy.md line 17 makes the same 30-day promise in public, so the document and the job agree with each other and both fall 150 days short.
findings.recommendation: Retain the registration fields for 180 days after closure in a restricted store, delete sessions and follows as now, and change the Privacy Policy sentence to match. Have counsel settle the DPDP overlap first.

findings.issue: image_to_image() calls model.edit() with 0 safety checks: neither safety.check_prompt() on the instruction nor safety.check_output() on the result. text_to_image() on lines 19 to 24 calls both, and services/imagine/safety.py blocks six topics at a 0.35 threshold and fails closed when the classifier is down. The rule needs technical measures on every path; here 1 of the 2 generation paths has none. It is the path where a real person's photo enters: its docstring says it can change what someone is wearing or doing, which is the route to non-consensual intimate imagery and to false depictions of real people.
findings.recommendation: Call safety.check_prompt(instruction, user) before model.edit() and safety.check_output(image) after it, and add a check on the source image. One wrapper that both modes pass through keeps a third mode from skipping the filter.

findings.issue: creators.clean_export is true. services/imagine/generate.py lines 12 to 13 skip the burned-in 'AI-generated' label when this flag is on and the user is a verified creator, so those users get Imagine images with no visible label. The rule needs a prominent label on every synthetic image and bars any feature that suppresses it. For every other user the label is burned into the pixels at generation; no gap was found there.
findings.recommendation: Set clean_export to false and remove the clean branch in _finish(), so the label is burned in for every user. If creators need a different placement, change the position, not the presence.

findings.issue: prepare_for_feed() runs codec.drop_metadata() on every post, whatever its source, and api/posts.py line 15 sends Imagine images through it. That strips the XMP provenance that services/imagine/provenance.py writes at generation (generator id, per-asset id, mode), so every Imagine image published to the feed and the CDN carries 0 provenance fields and no unique identifier; the rule bars removing either. Dropping EXIF from ordinary uploads is a privacy step and not a gap. The gap is generated media passing through the same step. Together with F-0012, a verified creator's Imagine post reaches the feed with neither label nor metadata.
findings.recommendation: When the source is imagine, carry the neem: XMP fields through the pipeline: read them before drop_metadata() and write them back onto each rendition after encoding, or exempt those fields from the drop. Add a test that a posted Imagine rendition still returns its asset id from provenance.read().

findings.issue: The only postal address published is in Singapore, under the parent company's name, and line 24 says legal notices should be sent there; the rule needs a physical contact address in India, published, for receiving communications. The README and the Terms name the operator as an Indian company in Bengaluru, and the two officers on the same page are stated as based in Bengaluru, but 0 Indian addresses appear in the templates and legal documents reviewed.
findings.recommendation: Publish a physical address in India on the Contact and grievance pages as the address for communications and legal notices, and point the legal-orders runbook at it.

findings.issue: The post form has 4 inputs (photo, caption, audience, allow comments) and 0 that ask whether the content is synthetically generated; the rule needs that declaration from the user before upload. api/posts.py reads no such field, and the posts table in db/schema.sql (lines 19 to 31) has no column to hold it: source records only whether the image came from an upload or from Imagine, and the server sets it.
findings.recommendation: Add a required declaration to the form, store it on the post in a new column, and refuse a post that leaves it unanswered. The server marking Imagine posts does not cover images made with other tools and then uploaded.

findings.issue: An uploaded image goes from the request straight to the media pipeline and is inserted with status live. 0 checks run on whether it is synthetic: no detector is called and no provenance metadata is read, and the pipeline then drops all metadata (services/media/pipeline.py line 11), so a later check has nothing to read. The rule needs technical measures that verify the user's declaration before publication, and a clear label on content that the declaration or the check shows to be synthetic. No label field or label step for uploaded content was found. post_card.html, the template that renders a post, was not in the reviewed material.
findings.recommendation: Before prepare_for_feed(), read provenance metadata (C2PA, XMP) from the upload and run a synthetic-image detector, store the result beside the declaration, and render a label on the post when either says synthetic.

findings.issue: The terms_reminder cron is '0 9 15 1 *', which fires once a year, at 09:00 on 15 January; the rule gives at least once every three months. The comment beside it says 'periodic'. Once a year was the period before 20 February 2026. The yearly notice in rule 3(1)(f) is met by the same job; this finding concerns the three-monthly notice only.
findings.recommendation: Change the cron to fire at least quarterly, such as '0 9 15 1,4,7,10 *', and keep the job_runs record as the log of sends.

findings.issue: The reminder body carries 1 of the 3 limbs the rule lists. Line 10 says content may be removed or the account suspended or closed straight away, which is limb (i). It does not say that a user responsible for unlawful information may face penalty or punishment under the IT Act or other law (limb (ii)), or that offences which must be reported, such as under the BNSS 2023 or the POCSO Act, will be reported to the appropriate authority (limb (iii)). The in-app card links to /terms, and the Terms carry neither statement; the Community Guidelines mention reporting only for child sexual abuse material.
findings.recommendation: Add two sentences to BODY covering limbs (ii) and (iii) in plain words, and mirror them in section 4 of the Terms.

findings.issue: Section 3 of the Terms tells users to 'use Imagine responsibly' and not to mislead people. It carries 0 of the 2 statements the rule needs: (i) that using Imagine to make unlawful synthetic content may attract penalty or punishment under the law, and (ii) that a contravention may lead to removal of the content, suspension or termination of the account, disclosure of the user's identity to a victim complainant in accordance with law, and mandatory reporting. Section 4 mentions removal and suspension in general terms only. The AI line in the Community Guidelines and the reminder in jobs/terms_reminder.py say nothing on either point. The Imagine screen (imagine.html) and its help page were not in the reviewed material, so any warning shown there was not seen.
findings.recommendation: Add both statements to section 3 of the Terms, show them on the Imagine screen before first use, and include them in the three-monthly reminder.

findings.issue: remove_for_policy() disables the post through disable_content() and returns. It makes 0 notification calls; the rule needs the user told beforehand of the action and the reasons, and given a chance to dispute it and ask for reinstatement, with the Resident Grievance Officer overseeing that mechanism. No dispute or reinstatement route for the author was found in the routes, templates or Terms. The copyright path on lines 28 to 32 does email the owner with a counter-notice link, but after the removal. With no Resident Grievance Officer named (F-0005), nobody is shown overseeing a dispute mechanism.
findings.recommendation: Send the author a notice naming the guideline and the reason before disable_content() runs in remove_for_policy(), add an appeal route that can reinstate the post, and name the Resident Grievance Officer as its owner.

findings.issue: A step for carrying out an order of the Grievance Appellate Committee, and for uploading a report of that on the website, was not found in the reviewed material. docs/runbooks/legal-orders.md covers court orders and government notices only, and the monthly report template has no section for Committee orders. The closure email and the grievance page do tell users about the appeal route, so a user can reach the Committee; what happens when its order comes back is undocumented.
findings.recommendation: Add a section on Committee orders to the legal-orders runbook: who receives them, who carries them out, and where the report is posted (the /transparency page already holds the monthly reports).

findings.issue: Measures to proactively identify depictions of rape or child sexual abuse, and copies of content already removed under rule 3(1)(d), were not found in the reviewed material. api/posts.py inserts an upload as live with 0 hash-match or classifier calls on that path. services/moderation/takedown.py refers to a classifier and jobs/compliance_report.py counts automated removals, so some automated tooling exists outside the files reviewed; its coverage, the notice shown to users, the human oversight and the periodic review of the tools could not be seen. Rated low for that reason. jobs/purge_removed.py deletes removed media after 30 days, and no retained hash was seen that a re-upload could be matched against.
findings.recommendation: Document the tools in use against the four parts of the rule: what they detect, the notice a user sees, who reviews their decisions, and the date of the last accuracy and bias review. Keep a hash of content removed on an order so a re-upload can be matched.

not_checked: DPDP Act 2023 and DPDP Rules 2025 (use Vigil)
IT Rules Part III (digital media publishers) and rule 5
Online gaming provisions: rule 3(1)(b)(ix)-(x), rule 4(10)-(13), rules 4A to 4C
Rule 3(1)(i), (k), (l), (m), (n): security practices, CERT-In reporting, accessibility, constitutional rights
Rule 4(2) first originator, rule 4(3) advertised content, rule 4(7) voluntary verification
The parts of rule 3(1)(d) other than the three-hour clock (G.S.R. 775(E) was not read when the catalog was built)
E-Commerce Rules beyond grievance duties
RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, TRAI and other sector rules
Any amendment notified after G.S.R. 120(E) of 10 February 2026
Whether the product is an intermediary in law: the classification records the user's answer and what the code shows
The live site: no URL was given, so no public page was fetched. Every finding on published details rests on the templates in the repo.
The seven E-Commerce Rules entries in the catalog (EC-4-2, EC-4-4, EC-4-5, EC-5-3-b, EC-5-3-c, EC-7-1-a, EC-7-1-f): the classification has no ecom tag, so /ecom did not run.
The classification itself: nobody was available to answer, so the tags rest on README.md and the code. The ssmi tag rests on the README's figure of about 62 lakh registered users in India.
tests/fixtures/grievances.json: not opened. The check skills bar opening complaint data and fixtures.

Templates and pages the repo refers to but does not contain: base.html, post_card.html, transparency.html, imagine.html, and the pages at /help/imagine, /help/legal/law-enforcement, /help/legal/copyright and /help/report/status. Whether the feed shows a label on Imagine posts, what the Imagine screen warns, and what the published transparency and status pages look like were not seen.

Modules imported but not supplied: the Imagine classifier, model, label and assets modules, the XMP and codec helpers, and the db, mailer, paging, publisher, notices, storage and flags services. Their behaviour was taken from how the reviewed code calls them.
The signup screen and the Android app: whether the three documents and the Grievance Officer's details are reachable from them was not seen.

How a complaint emailed to the grievance address gets a ticket number, an acknowledgement and a due time: the intake code handles the web form only, and no mail-ingest code was in the reviewed material.

Rule 3(1)(cb) account action: a report category, a 24x7 queue and a removal path for synthetic media were seen; code paths for account suspension, identity disclosure to a victim and mandatory reporting were not in the reviewed material.
Whether the Chief Compliance Officer and the nodal contact person are in fact appointed, employed and resident in India: only the Contact page's statements were read.
Registers and logs: the orders register, the law enforcement requests register, the job_runs record of reminder sends and past published reports were not supplied or not opened.
disclaimer: nodal is compliance tooling, not legal advice. It reports gaps visible in the material reviewed and never certifies compliance. Have a qualified lawyer check every finding before relying on it.
